question: Mental health challenges are increasing at an alarming rate in the EU. While awareness is growing and access to treatment improving, more potential side effects of medications are also being revealed. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) are the two most common antidepressants.

While they are helpful for many patients, these drugs can also cause severe side effects. One of them is post-SSRI sexual dysfunction (PSSD). Its symptom onset often follows cessation of serotonergic antidepressants. Symptoms can include genital anaesthesia, erectile dysfunction and orgasmic or ejaculatory anhedonia, but also non-sexual symptoms such as anhedonia and apathy.
Since SSRI and SNRI medications are also prescribed to very young patients, it is important to be aware of and actively prevent their side effects. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the growing issue of PSSD symptoms and their long-lasting effects on certain patients?
What measures will the Commission take to improve research on SSRI and SNRI medications so as to prevent PSSD?

How will the Commission work with the European Medicines Agency to ensure that doctors and patients are more aware of the risk of PSSD and ensure that the European Medicines Agency takes action based on the adverse drug reaction reports related to SSRIs and SNRIs?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2024) The Commission is aware that selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) may cause symptoms of sexual dysfunction, with some reports of symptoms continuing despite discontinuation of the treatment.

The product information of SSRIs and SNRIs is updated to inform patients that, in some cases, side effects of sexual dysfunction may be long-lasting or persistent. Patients with untreated depression could already experience some type of sexual dysfunction prior to treatment and even more serious consequences if not treated.

For the authorised SSRIs and SNRIs, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) has concluded the benefits risk ratio as positive. One of the priorities of Cluster 1 ‘Health’1 of Horizon Europe, the EU Framework Programme for Research and Innovation2, is the development of more effective preventative, diagnostic, therapeutic and monitoring strategies for diseases.

This includes more effective treatments for mental disorders. Researchers should be able to find opportunities for funding research related to post-SSRI sexual dysfunction through Horizon Europe, as call topics are generally broad and disease/disorder agnostic. All calls for proposals are published on the ‘EU Funding & Tenders’ portal3.

Following recommendations of the EMA based on the latest available scientific data, the Commission regularly updates the product information of SSRIs and SNRIs to ensure patient safety and to enable patients to make an informed decision about these treatments.
Patients can report side effects to their national medicine regulator, to the medicine manufacturer or to their doctor, nurse or pharmacist, who will inform regulators.
